flashcards.q: Give bytes-per-parameter for fp32, fp16/bf16, fp8, int8, int4/nf4.
flashcards.a: fp32=4, fp16/bf16=2, fp8=1, int8=1, int4/nf4=0.5 bytes per parameter.

flashcards.q: Why does quantization speed up decode more than prefill?
flashcards.a: Decode at low batch size is memory-bandwidth-bound (~1 FLOP per byte read, ~100-200x below the compute/bandwidth ridge point on H100-class GPUs) so shrinking weight bytes speeds it up roughly proportionally. Prefill reuses weights across many tokens in parallel and is compute-bound, so it needs real INT8/FP8 tensor-core throughput (weight+activation quant), not just smaller weight bytes.

flashcards.q: PTQ vs QAT: what's the difference and when is QAT worth it?
flashcards.a: PTQ quantizes an already-trained model using a small calibration set (128-512 samples), cheap, no retraining -- the default. QAT simulates quantization noise during training so weights adapt to tolerate it; worth it only for sub-4-bit targets when already running a fine-tuning pipeline.

flashcards.q: GPTQ vs AWQ: mechanism difference and 2026 default.
flashcards.a: GPTQ uses layer-wise Hessian-based error correction (quantize a weight, adjust the rest of the layer to compensate). AWQ identifies salient weight channels via ACTIVATION magnitude and protects them with per-channel scaling. AWQ is the 2026 GPU-serving default -- better quality at 4-bit, especially on instruction-tuned models.

flashcards.q: Measured HumanEval degradation at 4-bit: fp16 baseline vs AWQ/GGUF vs GPTQ.
flashcards.a: fp16 baseline 56.1%. AWQ and GGUF both ~51.8% (~4pt loss). GPTQ trails at ~46% (~10pt loss).

flashcards.q: Why are activations harder to quantize than weights in LLMs?
flashcards.a: Weight distributions are uniform and well-behaved. Activations develop systematic outlier channels, 20-100x larger than the rest, in fixed feature dimensions across nearly every token, once models exceed ~6-7B params. A max-based INT8 scale either clips the outliers (losing signal) or wastes precision accommodating them.

flashcards.q: State SmoothQuant's rescaling identity and why it's exact, not approximate.
flashcards.a: (X/s)(sW) = XW for any per-channel scale s. Dividing activations by s and multiplying the corresponding weight channel by s leaves the matmul output unchanged -- it migrates quantization difficulty from activations to weights via an exact algebraic identity, not a lossy approximation.

flashcards.q: What does GGUF add beyond being another 4-bit format?
flashcards.a: A self-contained file format for llama.cpp with multiple quant levels per tensor (Q2_K-Q8_0); k-quants mix precision within a block, keeping a minority of important values at higher precision. Dominant for CPU/edge/consumer-GPU inference, not GPU-cluster serving.

flashcards.q: Rank task categories by how much they degrade under aggressive quantization, easiest to hardest.
flashcards.a: Chat/summarization (most tolerant) < long-context retrieval / multilingual (especially low-resource languages) < math/code (degrades first and hardest, because compounding multi-step errors invalidate the whole output).

flashcards.q: KV cache quantization: give the rough quality cost of INT8, FP8, and INT4.
flashcards.a: INT8: holds accuracy well across most tasks. FP8: typically under 0.5 percentage points on long-context retrieval benchmarks. INT4: real, growing degradation with context length and reasoning depth, because per-step error compounds across every subsequent attention read of the cache.

flashcards.q: Why does calibration data choice matter for GPTQ/AWQ?
flashcards.a: Both derive quantization parameters (Hessian stats or salient channels) from a calibration set of ~128-512 samples. Calibrating on a generic corpus when production traffic is domain-specific (code, a non-English language) means the wrong channels get protected, causing degradation invisible on general benchmarks.

flashcards.q: Weight-only vs weight-and-activation quantization: when does each matter?
flashcards.a: Weight-only (GPTQ/AWQ/GGUF/NF4) shrinks bytes read from HBM -- helps memory-bound decode, but the matmul still runs at higher precision after dequant, so it doesn't unlock faster compute. Weight-and-activation (SmoothQuant W8A8, FP8) engages real INT8/FP8 tensor-core throughput, needed for compute-bound regimes like large-batch prefill.

flashcards.q: What is the LLM.int8() mixed-precision decomposition?
flashcards.a: Identify the small set of outlier activation feature dimensions per forward pass, compute those specific columns in fp16 and everything else in INT8, then recombine -- correct but adds overhead proportional to how many outlier dimensions appear.

flashcards.q: Why is decode's arithmetic intensity roughly 1 FLOP/byte at batch size 1?
flashcards.a: Each decode step reads the entire weight matrix from HBM once and performs on the order of one FLOP of matmul work per byte read (e.g. a 70B fp16 model reads 140GB and does ~140 GFLOPs per token) -- far below the ridge point where GPU compute would become the bottleneck.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT quantize at all?
flashcards.a: When you have ample GPU memory headroom, the workload is latency-insensitive at your actual batch sizes, or reproducibility against a known fp16 baseline matters more than memory savings -- the validation cost (calibration, task-specific eval, KV-cache-specific testing) of doing it correctly is real.
